det.desc: Fioriware pottery bowl (dark blue/cobalt) Fioriware was made in Zanesville, Ohio from 1987 to 2006. I bought this vintage bowl new circa 1990 at the Fioriware shop in downtown Zanesville. I had several designs but I only have this bowl design in this color (and a light blue bowl in another listing on here) and style. Unfortunately these are the only two examples I have left. The bowl is approximately 6 inches across. The Fioriware makers mark on the bottom is pretty clear, as seen in the photo. The stamp says "Fioriware Art Pottery Made in Zanesville Ohio". Fioriware is considered very collectible and an online search will show that most Fioriware items for sale online are their famous Majolica-style ceramics. These types of bowls were more a utilitarian line (which is why I only have two left) and I have kept this bowl and its light blue partner out of use in a cabinet for many years. The bowl is used but in excellent condition, as can be seen in the photos.

rows.t: Antique quadruple plate item marked "Union Met Works".

det.desc: Quadruple plate refers to a type of silver-plated metalware where the base metal is coated with four times the amount of silver typically used in standard silver plating. This process was popular in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, offering a more durable and luxurious finish than single or double plate, making it a more affordable alternative to solid silver. Items were often marked with terms like "Quadruple Plate" or "4x" to denote this higher quality plating. Union Metal Works was a manufacturer of silver-plated hollowware and flatware, operating primarily in the United States during the late 19th and early 20th centuries. They produced a range of household items, from serving spoons and forks to pitchers and trays, often featuring intricate designs characteristic of the Victorian and Edwardian eras. Their "Quadruple Plate" items are recognized by collectors for their craftsmanship and historical significance as examples of mass-produced, yet elegant, tableware.

rows.t: Japanese Cast Iron Teapot Square Kettle Antique

det.desc: This is a vintage Japanese Nanbu ironware cast iron tea kettle, also known as a tetsubin. Tetsubin are traditionally used for boiling water for making tea and are highly regarded for their durability and excellent heat retention. They are known to impart a gentle quality to water by releasing iron elements, which some believe enhances the taste of tea or coffee and provides a natural iron supplement. Authentic tetsubin, like the one pictured with its a bamboo-motif design, are often handcrafted by skilled artisans in the Iwate region of Japan, where this craft has a history spanning over 400 years. Unlike enamel-coated teapots used only for steeping, a tetsubin is a kettle designed to be placed directly on a heat source

rows.t: Antique coat of Arms Black Metal "GUN POWDER" Cylinder Canister w lid

det.desc: This is a large antique japanned (black-lacquered) metal gunpowder storage/display canister featuring the coat of arms and motto of Belfast. Identification • The gold lettering reads “GUN POWDER.” • The central heraldic design is the official coat of arms of Belfast (granted/confirmed 1890, though elements are earlier): a shield with a ship on waves, a pile of vair, and a canton with a bell, flanked by a wolf (dexter) and seahorse (sinister), with the crest of a seahorse and the motto “PRO TANTO QUID RETRIBUAMUS” (“What return shall we make for so much?” / “For so much, what shall we repay?” — from Psalm 116). These large cylindrical tins were typically used in 19th- or early-20th-century gunsmiths’ or sporting-goods shops for bulk black powder storage or as counter/display canisters. The Belfast arms strongly suggest an Irish (Northern Irish) origin or retail connection. Condition (from the photo) Visible surface wear, scratches, scuffs, and some loss to the japanning and gilt decoration are present, which is typical for age. rows.t: "Exodus (Main Theme)" Vintage Piano Solo Sheet Music Composed by Earnest Gold

det.desc: This is vintage sheet music for the "Exodus (Main Theme)", a celebrated piano solo composed by Ernest Gold. This theme was written for the 1960 epic film Exodus, directed by Otto Preminger, which depicts the founding of the modern state of Israel. The iconic cover art, characterized by its striking blue and white graphic of a hand holding a rifle with a ship in the background, was designed by the renowned artist Saul Bass. Ernest Gold's score for Exodus won the Academy Award for Best Original Score in 1960. The theme itself also won the Grammy Award for Song of the Year in 1961, making it the only instrumental piece to date to receive this honor. Beyond the film, the theme became a major commercial success. An instrumental version by Ferrante & Teicher reached number two on the Billboard Hot 100 in 1960. This specific sheet music was published by Chappell & Co. around the film's release in 1960
